snippet.title: Why Is It Called a Vaccine?
snippet.description:
Why Vaccines Are Named After a Cow
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ETynHpIYLeY

Twenty-two years before Edward Jenner's 1798 book, Benjamin Jesty tried cowpox in 1774. Jenner called the disease variolae vaccinae ("smallpox of the cow"), and from vacca, the Latin word for cow, came the name vaccination.

snippet.title: How Did We Discover the Periodic Table?
snippet.description:
Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in the periodic table? Because he trusted his pattern more than the list of known elements. In 1869 he left spaces for metals nobody had found, and predicted what they'd weigh. Then gallium, scandium and germanium turned up and fitted.

snippet.title: Why Vaccines Are Named After a Cow
snippet.description:
Every vaccine is named after a cow. How did the Edward Jenner cowpox vaccine conquer the deadly smallpox virus?
In 1796 a country doctor took cowpox from a milkmaid's hand and put it into a boy's arm, then tested whether smallpox could still touch him — the breakthrough behind every jab (and why can't every shot be a pill).

This film is how we found out: the dairy rumour that milkmaids never caught smallpox, Benjamin Jesty's family in 1774, Edward Jenner's test on James Phipps (14 May and 1 July 1796), the book that spread it (1798), and the word vaccine, from the Latin vacca, cow.

Chapters
0:00 The speckled monster
1:41 The milkmaids' secret
3:52 A pail, a lancet and a boy
5:13 The test
6:48 The word that saved millions

Sources
Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (London, 1798)
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, "Jenner, Edward"
World Health Organization, declaration of smallpox eradication (1980)

snippet.title: What's Really Inside an Atom?
snippet.description:
What's really inside an atom, and why is the periodic table in this order? Four discoveries, one century — from a knife and a gold coin to the number that fixed the table.

Cut gold in half, then again. How small can you go before it stops being gold? Dalton weighed atoms. Thomson found a piece inside them. Rutherford found their tiny centre. Moseley counted what was inside every element — and tellurium 52 finally sat before iodine 53 for a reason that wasn't weight.

A 3D cartoon film about the moment chemistry got a ruler that worked.

History of Science · Discovery. Wonder. Proof. · @HistoryOfScienceYT

#HistoryOfScience #Atom #PeriodicTable #AtomicNumber #Moseley #Rutherford #Thomson #Dalton

1:09 The table that broke its own rule
2:41 The crumb inside the atom
4:05 The shell that bounced back
5:55 Counting with X-rays

Sources: J. Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808); D. Mendeleev, Zeitschrift für Chemie 12 (1869); J. J. Thomson, "Cathode Rays", Philosophical Magazine 44 (1897); H. Geiger & E. Marsden, "On a Diffuse Reflection of the α-Particles", Proc. R. Soc. A 82 (1909); E. Rutherford, "The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom", Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911); H. G. J. Moseley, "The High-Frequency Spectra of the Elements", Philosophical Magazine 26 (1913).

snippet.description:
How did experiments explain blood, germs and atoms? Six discovery stories follow the evidence across almost three hundred years, from a tied arm and a willow tree to a swan-neck flask, the periodic table, X-rays and gold foil.

This 49-minute compilation brings together six History of Science films in chronological order of proof (1628 to 1911), with a new cold-open introduction, chapter cards, five bridges and an ink-drawn timeline.

Chapters
0:00 Six discoveries, one question
0:53 The Hidden Circle
9:23 Built From Air
17:57 The Invisible Enemy
24:14 The Empty Chairs
33:22 A Light Through Skin
40:27 Inside the Atom

Sources (The Hidden Circle): William Harvey, De Motu Cordis (Frankfurt, 1628), ch. 9, 11, 13 and dedication (cardiac output sum and forearm ligature proof); Hieronymus Fabricius, De Venarum Ostiolis (1603, one-way vein valves); Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica, 2nd ed. (1555, interventricular septum); Marcello Malpighi, De pulmonibus (1661, pulmonary capillaries); Geoffrey Keynes, The Life of William Harvey (1966); Vivian Nutton, Ancient Medicine (2004, Galenic system).

Sources (Built From Air): J. B. van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae (1648, five-year willow tree experiment); Stephen Hales, Vegetable Staticks (1727, leaf transpiration and air nourishment); Joseph Priestley, "Observations on Different Kinds of Air", Philosophical Transactions 62 (1772, mint restoring injured air); Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables (1779, sunlight oxygen production by green leaves); Jean Senebier, Mémoires physico-chymiques (1782, fixed air / CO₂ requirement); Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure, Recherches chimiques sur la végétation (1804, carbon mass balance).

Sources (The Invisible Enemy): Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1674–1677, microscopic organisms in water); Ignaz Semmelweis, Die Ätiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers (1861, handwashing and childbed fever); Louis Pasteur, "Mémoire sur les corpuscules organisés qui existent dans l'atmosphère", Annales des Sciences Naturelles 16 (1861, swan-neck flask experiments); Joseph Lister, "On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery", The Lancet 90 (1867, carbolic acid antisepsis).

Sources (The Empty Chairs): Antoine Lavoisier, Traité Élémentaire de Chimie (1789, simple substances); J. W. Döbereiner, Annalen der Physik 15 (1829, triads) & J. A. R. Newlands, Chemical News 12 (1865, octaves); Stanislao Cannizzaro, Sunto di un corso di filosofia chimica (1858 / Karlsruhe Congress 1860, atomic weights); Dmitri Mendeleev, Zeitschrift für Chemie 12 (1869, periodic table and predicted gaps); P.-É. Lecoq de Boisbaudran, Comptes Rendus 81 (1875, gallium), L. F. Nilson, Comptes Rendus 88 (1879, scandium) & C. Winkler, Berichte 19 (1886, germanium).

Sources (A Light Through Skin): William Crookes, Philosophical Transactions 170 (1879, cathode-ray tubes); Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, "Über eine neue Art von Strahlen", Sitzungsberichte der Physikalisch-Medizinischen Gesellschaft zu Würzburg (Dec 1895 & Mar 1896, barium platinocyanide screen fluorescence and Bertha Röntgen's hand radiograph); W. C. Röntgen (trans. A. Stanton), "On a New Kind of Rays", Nature 53 (Jan 1896, early medical radiography); Nobel Foundation, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen Biographical (1901 Nobel Prize in Physics).

Sources (Inside the Atom): John Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808, relative atomic weights); Dmitri Mendeleev, Zeitschrift für Chemie 12 (1869, tellurium–iodine weight inversion); J. J. Thomson, "Cathode Rays", Philosophical Magazine 44 (1897, electron charge-to-mass ratio); Hans Geiger & Ernest Marsden, "On a Diffuse Reflection of the α-Particles", Proceedings of the Royal Society A 82 (1909, gold-foil back-scattering); Ernest Rutherford, "The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom", Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911, atomic nucleus); H. G. J. Moseley, "The High-Frequency Spectra of the Elements", Philosophical Magazine 26 (1913, atomic number).

Pictures: AI-generated 3D scenes. Narration uses a synthetic version of Ben’s voice. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.

snippet.title: The Willow Tree That Was Made of Air
snippet.description:
A fully grown tree is built almost entirely out of thin air. So where does a tree's weight really come from?
For 2,000 years people believed plants ate the soil, until a willow in a pot, a sprig of mint and a sunny window revealed photosynthesis.

This film is how we found out: van Helmont's five-year willow (169 pounds of tree, two ounces of soil gone), the gas he named and never connected, Priestley's mint that repaired the air (1771), Ingenhousz's bubbles in sunlight (1779), and the carbon Senebier and de Saussure traced to the air.

Chapters
0:00 Plants eat soil
1:02 Five years and two ounces
2:59 The air that mint repaired
4:34 Bubbles in the sunlight
6:06 Carbon from the sky

Sources
J. B. van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae (1648)
Stephen Hales, Vegetable Staticks (1727)
Joseph Priestley, "Observations on Different Kinds of Air", Philosophical Transactions 62 (1772)
Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables (1779)
Jean Senebier, Mémoires physico-chymiques (1782)
Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure, Recherches chimiques sur la végétation (1804)
Geerdt Magiels, From Sunlight to Insight (2010)

snippet.title: How Did We Discover X-rays?
snippet.description:
X-rays let us see through skin. This is how Röntgen found them: a tube wrapped in black cardboard, a screen across a dark room that glowed when it shouldn't have, and a wedding ring on the first plate.

In a Würzburg lab in 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen chased a glow that had no business being there, and named the unknown ray X.

This is the story of how we discovered X-rays: the cardboard that should have stayed dark, the living bones seen without a knife, and Bertha Röntgen’s hand — bones and wedding ring — that turned a haunted glow into proof the world could not argue with.

Chapters
0:00 A Dark Lab, 1895
1:27 The Cardboard
2:32 Bones Without a Knife
3:59 Bertha’s Ring
5:25 A New Kind of Seeing

snippet.title: How Did Experiments Explain Blood, Germs and Atoms?
snippet.description:
How did experiments explain blood, germs and atoms? Six discovery stories follow the evidence across almost three hundred years, from a tied arm and a willow tree to a swan-neck flask, the periodic table, X-rays and gold foil.

This 49-minute compilation brings together six History of Science films in chronological order of proof (1628 to 1911), with a new cold-open introduction, chapter cards, five bridges and an ink-drawn timeline.

Chapters
0:00 Six discoveries, one question
0:53 The Hidden Circle
9:23 Built From Air
17:57 The Invisible Enemy
24:14 The Empty Chairs
33:22 A Light Through Skin
40:27 Inside the Atom

Sources (The Hidden Circle): William Harvey, De Motu Cordis (Frankfurt, 1628), ch. 9, 11, 13 and dedication (cardiac output sum and forearm ligature proof); Hieronymus Fabricius, De Venarum Ostiolis (1603, one-way vein valves); Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica, 2nd ed. (1555, interventricular septum); Marcello Malpighi, De pulmonibus (1661, pulmonary capillaries); Geoffrey Keynes, The Life of William Harvey (1966); Vivian Nutton, Ancient Medicine (2004, Galenic system).

Sources (Built From Air): J. B. van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae (1648, five-year willow tree experiment); Stephen Hales, Vegetable Staticks (1727, leaf transpiration and air nourishment); Joseph Priestley, "Observations on Different Kinds of Air", Philosophical Transactions 62 (1772, mint restoring injured air); Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables (1779, sunlight oxygen production by green leaves); Jean Senebier, Mémoires physico-chymiques (1782, fixed air / CO₂ requirement); Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure, Recherches chimiques sur la végétation (1804, carbon mass balance).

Sources (The Invisible Enemy): Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1674–1677, microscopic organisms in water); Ignaz Semmelweis, Die Ätiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers (1861, handwashing and childbed fever); Louis Pasteur, "Mémoire sur les corpuscules organisés qui existent dans l'atmosphère", Annales des Sciences Naturelles 16 (1861, swan-neck flask experiments); Joseph Lister, "On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery", The Lancet 90 (1867, carbolic acid antisepsis).

Sources (The Empty Chairs): Antoine Lavoisier, Traité Élémentaire de Chimie (1789, simple substances); J. W. Döbereiner, Annalen der Physik 15 (1829, triads) & J. A. R. Newlands, Chemical News 12 (1865, octaves); Stanislao Cannizzaro, Sunto di un corso di filosofia chimica (1858 / Karlsruhe Congress 1860, atomic weights); Dmitri Mendeleev, Zeitschrift für Chemie 12 (1869, periodic table and predicted gaps); P.-É. Lecoq de Boisbaudran, Comptes Rendus 81 (1875, gallium), L. F. Nilson, Comptes Rendus 88 (1879, scandium) & C. Winkler, Berichte 19 (1886, germanium).

Sources (A Light Through Skin): William Crookes, Philosophical Transactions 170 (1879, cathode-ray tubes); Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, "Über eine neue Art von Strahlen", Sitzungsberichte der Physikalisch-Medizinischen Gesellschaft zu Würzburg (Dec 1895 & Mar 1896, barium platinocyanide screen fluorescence and Bertha Röntgen's hand radiograph); W. C. Röntgen (trans. A. Stanton), "On a New Kind of Rays", Nature 53 (Jan 1896, early medical radiography); Nobel Foundation, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen Biographical (1901 Nobel Prize in Physics).

Sources (Inside the Atom): John Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808, relative atomic weights); Dmitri Mendeleev, Zeitschrift für Chemie 12 (1869, tellurium–iodine weight inversion); J. J. Thomson, "Cathode Rays", Philosophical Magazine 44 (1897, electron charge-to-mass ratio); Hans Geiger & Ernest Marsden, "On a Diffuse Reflection of the α-Particles", Proceedings of the Royal Society A 82 (1909, gold-foil back-scattering); Ernest Rutherford, "The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom", Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911, atomic nucleus); H. G. J. Moseley, "The High-Frequency Spectra of the Elements", Philosophical Magazine 26 (1913, atomic number).

Pictures: AI-generated 3D scenes. Narration uses a synthetic version of Ben’s voice. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.

B. van Helmont, Ortus Medicinae (1648, five-year willow tree experiment); Stephen Hales, Vegetable Staticks (1727, leaf transpiration and air nourishment); Joseph Priestley, "Observations on Different Kinds of Air", Philosophical Transactions 62 (1772, mint restoring injured air); Jan Ingenhousz, Experiments upon Vegetables (1779, sunlight oxygen production by green leaves); Jean Senebier, Mémoires physico-chymiques (1782, fixed air / CO₂ requirement); Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure, Recherches chimiques sur la végétation (1804, carbon mass balance).

Sources (The Invisible Enemy): Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1674–1677, microscopic organisms in water); Ignaz Semmelweis, Die Ätiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers (1861, handwashing and childbed fever); Louis Pasteur, "Mémoire sur les corpuscules organisés qui existent dans l'atmosphère", Annales des Sciences Naturelles 16 (1861, swan-neck flask experiments); Joseph Lister, "On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery", The Lancet 90 (1867, carbolic acid antisepsis).

Sources (The Empty Chairs): Antoine Lavoisier, Traité Élémentaire de Chimie (1789, simple substances); J. W. Döbereiner, Annalen der Physik 15 (1829, triads) & J. A. R. Lecoq de Boisbaudran, Comptes Rendus 81 (1875, gallium), L. F. Nilson, Comptes Rendus 88 (1879, scandium) & C. Winkler, Berichte 19 (1886, germanium).

Sources (A Light Through Skin): William Crookes, Philosophical Transactions 170 (1879, cathode-ray tubes); Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, "Über eine neue Art von Strahlen", Sitzungsberichte der Physikalisch-Medizinischen Gesellschaft zu Würzburg (Dec 1895 & Mar 1896, barium platinocyanide screen fluorescence and Bertha Röntgen's hand radiograph); W. C. Röntgen (trans. A. Stanton), "On a New Kind of Rays", Nature 53 (Jan 1896, early medical radiography); Nobel Foundation, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen Biographical (1901 Nobel Prize in Physics).

Sources (Inside the Atom): John Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808, relative atomic weights); Dmitri Mendeleev, Zeitschrift für Chemie 12 (1869, tellurium–iodine weight inversion); J. J. Thomson, "Cathode Rays", Philosophical Magazine 44 (1897, electron charge-to-mass ratio); Hans Geiger & Ernest Marsden, "On a Diffuse Reflection of the α-Particles", Proceedings of the Royal Society A 82 (1909, gold-foil back-scattering); Ernest Rutherford, "The Scattering of α and β Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom", Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911, atomic nucleus); H. G. J. Moseley, "The High-Frequency Spectra of the Elements", Philosophical Magazine 26 (1913, atomic number).

snippet.title: Are Marie Curie's Notebooks Still Radioactive?
snippet.description:
Yes. Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive, and her papers are kept in lead-lined boxes in Paris.

snippet.title: The Tied Arm That Proved Your Blood Circulates
snippet.description:
Your heart pumps more blood in half an hour than your whole body holds. So where does it all go?
For 1,400 years doctors taught that blood was made from food and used up, until William Harvey proved it circulates, with a sum and a band tied round an arm.

This film is how he did it: Galen's liver, Fabricius's little doors in the veins, Harvey's sum at the Royal College of Physicians, the tied arm in De Motu Cordis (1628), and the capillaries Malpighi found in 1661.

Chapters
